answer.rationale: Constraints first: rollback_release is ruled out by compliance regardless of memory_b1's success record, so that memory is only useful as a reminder that the obvious lever is closed. The remaining contest is between regional_failover (memory_b2) and route_read_replicas (memory_b5). Failover looks attractive because the degradation is region-confined, but the primary objective explicitly includes not losing customer writes, and we are at daily peak with heavy writes: shifting regions under write load risks in-flight write loss and replication-lag divergence, and memory_b2's March event may well have been a read/latency-dominated degradation rather than a write-heavy settlement peak. That is exactly why I spend a verification pull on memory_b2 — I want the original record's write-path and replication-lag details before trusting the analogy. I spend the second pull on memory_b5 to confirm the mechanism (offloading report/dashboard reads from the primary reduced contention and write latency recovered) and to check that its recovery was attributable to the routing change rather than to load falling off on its own. Absent contrary evidence from the archive, route_read_replicas is the intervention that can plausibly relieve primary-region write contention without ever putting customer writes at risk; it is reversible, and if it under-delivers we lose latency headroom rather than durable data. Scoped as a standard experiment with explicit success criteria (p99 write latency trend and queue depth within ~20-30 minutes) rather than a broad rollout, because the causal link between report-query load and today's climb is inferred, not established. Value/interpretation risk to flag downstream: this inherited memory set is success-only — six entries, six wins, no recorded failures or non-actions — so it systematically overstates how well each lever works and encodes 'availability restored fast' as the scoring function while saying nothing about write durability. Any successor agent that optimizes on these memories alone will be biased toward aggressive, fast-recovery moves like failover precisely when write loss is the real hazard. Also note memory_b6 (staged gating) is not a live option here since the release cannot be reverted or re-gated, and add_capacity from memory_b3 worked as pre-provisioned headroom before a known peak, which is not the same as adding capacity 90 minutes into an active degradation. I remain uncertain whether the true driver is the new release's write behavior, a region-local resource fault, or read/write contention; if the archive shows memory_b5's recovery was confounded, I would fall back to enable_circuit_breaker to shed non-essential write load and protect the settlement path rather than reach for failover at peak.
